title: The loops: cerebellum, basal ganglia and gait
description: How the cerebellum and basal ganglia shape movement without powering it, how to localize ataxia, vertigo and involuntary movements, and why watching a child walk is the best single test of the motor system.
why: The cerebellum and basal ganglia shape movement without weakening it, and their disorders show most clearly when a child walks.
objectives: Explain why cerebellar and basal ganglia disease spare strength, and check strength before calling a movement ataxic.
Localize cerebellar signs by side and by midline versus hemisphere.
Work through acute ataxia in a child in order of danger and likelihood.
Describe involuntary movements precisely, and read a gait as a tour of the levels of the neuraxis.

sections.title: The cerebellum and basal ganglia work in loops
sections.content:
Neither the cerebellum nor the basal ganglia sends fibers to the anterior horn cells, so neither moves anything on its own. Both work in loops that take in what the cortex intends and what the body reports and send their output back through the thalamus to the motor cortex that will act on it. The cerebellum is "the great modulator of the nervous system" (Pearl 2014, p. 116), and the phrase fits the basal ganglia too. The cerebellar loop tunes the accuracy and timing of movement. The basal ganglia loop sets how much movement is allowed and how fast it runs.

**Test strength before coordination**

Because these loops shape movement without powering it, their disease leaves **strength intact**. A child with cerebellar disease is clumsy, overshoots and walks on a broad base, yet pushes against your hand normally. A child with basal ganglia disease has too little movement or too much of the wrong kind, but no paralysis. Prove that a limb is strong before you call its movement ataxic or dystonic, because a weak arm also misses the target and a weak child also falls. That is why the [[m03-first-fork|first fork]] comes before any question about coordination.

**Cerebellar and basal ganglia signs**

- **Cerebellar** disorders produce errors in range, rate and rhythm, seen as dysmetria on finger-nose testing, irregular rapid alternating movements, an intention tremor that grows as the hand approaches the target, a wide-based gait, nystagmus and scanning speech (Pearl 2014, pp. 63, 116).
- **Basal ganglia** disorders produce errors in amount and selection, with slowness and rigidity at one end and chorea, dystonia, tics and other unwanted movements at the other.

Tremor is a practical way to tell the two apart. A cerebellar tremor appears on action and worsens near the target, and a tremor at rest belongs to the basal ganglia.

**In a child**

Clumsiness is one of the commonest reasons a child is referred. Most clumsy children have no cerebellar or basal ganglia lesion, and many have developmental coordination disorder. The first question is whether the clumsiness is simply normal for the child's age. The toddler's broad-based, jerky, falling gait is normal at the age when walking begins (DeMyer, p. 338).
keyPoints: The cerebellum and basal ganglia work in loops back to the motor cortex, shaping movement without powering it.
Because their disease spares strength, a limb must be shown to be strong before its movement is called ataxic or dystonic.
Cerebellar errors are errors of range, rate and rhythm, and basal ganglia errors are errors of amount and selection.
An action tremor that worsens near the target is cerebellar, and a tremor at rest comes from the basal ganglia.

question.question: A 7-year-old overshoots badly on finger-nose testing with the right arm. Strength in that arm is 3 out of 5, with brisk right reflexes. What is the most defensible description?
options: Right cerebellar ataxia, calling for imaging of the posterior fossa
Right arm weakness of upper motor neuron type, which means the overshoot cannot be called cerebellar while the limb is this weak
question.explanation: Coordination can only be judged in a limb strong enough to do the task. Power of 3 out of 5 with brisk reflexes is upper motor neuron weakness, and weakness alone makes movements inaccurate, so calling the overshoot cerebellar would send you to the wrong level. Chorea is a random, flowing extra movement. Normal clumsiness does not come with one-sided weakness and brisk reflexes.

sections.title: Localizing within the cerebellum
sections.content:
The first of the cerebellum's localizing rules often surprises students. **Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion** (Pearl 2014, p. 63), and a lesion of one side of the cerebellum causes cerebellar signs only on that side (DeMyer, p. 339).

**Signs on the same side**

The explanation is a double crossing of the pathway. Cerebellar output leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses in the midbrain to reach the opposite thalamus and motor cortex. The corticospinal tract from that cortex crosses back in the medulla, to the side where the cerebellar output began. The two crossings cancel out, so a lesion of one cerebellar hemisphere, or of its outflow before the first crossing, shows its clumsiness on its own side. A midbrain lesion after the crossing gives ataxia of the opposite limbs, as in Benedikt syndrome.

**Midline and hemisphere lesions**

The midline vermis and the flocculonodular lobe look after the trunk, stance and eye movements, and the hemispheres plan and tune the limbs (Pearl 2014, p. 63). The pattern of ataxia follows that division.

- **Midline lesions** give truncal ataxia, with axial unsteadiness and a wide-based, staggering gait but little ataxia of the limbs when they are tested lying down (Brazis 2011, pp. 411-412). They often bring nystagmus, vertigo, nausea and vomiting as well (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
- **Hemispheric lesions** give limb ataxia on the same side, with dysmetria, intention tremor and poor rapid alternating movements (Brazis 2011, p. 412).
- **Both at once**, a pancerebellar syndrome, suggests something diffuse, such as a toxin or drug, a metabolic or inherited disorder, or multiple sclerosis (DeMyer, p. 339).

:::deeper Is cerebellar output inhibitory?
Cerebellar output is sometimes described as entirely inhibitory (Pearl 2014, p. 63). That is true of the cerebellar cortex's own output, from the Purkinje cells to the deep nuclei. The deep nuclei carry the cerebellum's message to the rest of the brain, and all their projections are excitatory except those to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405). A cerebellar lesion therefore leaves the thalamus and motor cortex with less excitatory drive instead of releasing them.
:::

**In a child**

The caudal vermis syndrome, in which the child staggers while the limbs are relatively spared, is typical of a medulloblastoma, the classic midline tumor of childhood (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A child who walks badly but does heel-shin well lying down has already pointed you to the midline.
keyPoints: Cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion (Pearl 2014, p. 63), because the outflow pathway crosses twice.
Midline lesions give truncal and gait ataxia with relatively spared limbs, and hemispheric lesions give limb ataxia on the same side (Brazis 2011, pp. 411-412).
Bilateral, pancerebellar signs suggest a diffuse cause such as a toxin, a drug, or a metabolic, inherited or demyelinating disorder (DeMyer, p. 339).
The deep nuclei carry the cerebellar output and are excitatory except in their projections to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405), and only the Purkinje stage before them is inhibitory.

question.question: A 5-year-old has a month of morning vomiting and now staggers and sways when standing, on a broad base. Lying down, finger-nose and heel-shin are nearly normal on both sides. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: The cerebellar vermis in the midline
The dorsal columns of the spinal cord
question.explanation: Ataxia of stance and gait with fairly spared limbs is the midline pattern, and with morning vomiting it raises a midline posterior fossa tumor blocking the fourth ventricle, such as a medulloblastoma (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A right hemispheric lesion would show right limb ataxia. Dorsal column ataxia worsens with the eyes closed and loses position sense. Hemisphere disease would bring weakness or cognitive signs.

sections.title: Acute ataxia in a child
sections.content:
A child who could walk yesterday and staggers today is one of the commonest urgent problems in child neurology. The level is usually the cerebellum or its connections. The acute tempo narrows the mechanisms to a short list, which you work through in order of danger and of likelihood.

**The common causes**

- **An ingestion.** Assume that a toddler with sudden ataxia and drowsiness has taken something until there is good reason to think otherwise. Many sedatives and antiseizure drugs cause a pancerebellar picture.
- **Post-infectious cerebellar ataxia.** This immune-mediated ataxia follows a viral illness (Pearl 2014, p. 63), and it is the commonest cause of acute ataxia in young children. The child is alert, the ataxia is mostly truncal, and the rest of the exam is usually normal.
- **Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia.** An irritable child with chaotic, darting eye movements in every direction and jerks of the trunk and limbs has this pattern, and needs a search for a neuroblastoma.
- **A posterior fossa tumor.** The story is usually one of weeks rather than days, often with headache and vomiting from raised intracranial pressure (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A child who seems to have become ataxic overnight may have been compensating for longer.
- **Something outside the cerebellum.** Absent reflexes with ataxia point to the peripheral nerves, as in the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Lost position sense points to a sensory ataxia, and a weak leg can masquerade as ataxia.

**The first examination**

Start with the level of consciousness, and ask what medicines and substances are in the house. Look at the eyes for nystagmus and opsoclonus, and at the optic discs for papilledema. Check reflexes, position sense and strength to make sure the ataxia is truly cerebellar. A child who is drowsy or getting worse, or who has papilledema, focal signs or a severe headache, needs urgent imaging. An alert child with isolated truncal ataxia after a viral illness and an otherwise normal exam can often be watched closely.

Post-infectious ataxia is common enough that it is tempting to stop as soon as it seems to fit. Ask each of these questions anyway, because that is how the ingestion, the tumor and the neuroblastoma are found.
keyPoints: In a toddler with acute ataxia, especially with drowsiness, an ingestion should be considered first.
Post-infectious ataxia follows a viral illness in an alert child, with mostly truncal ataxia and an otherwise normal exam (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
Chaotic multidirectional eye movements with myoclonus suggest opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia, which should prompt a search for a neuroblastoma.
Drowsiness, papilledema, focal signs or a worsening course call for urgent imaging.

question.question: A 2-year-old has become unsteady over three days and is irritable. His eyes make rapid, chaotic, conjugate darting movements in all directions, and his trunk and limbs jerk. Reflexes are normal and there was no access to medicines. What should the next step include?
options: Reassurance and review in two weeks for post-infectious ataxia
Nerve conduction studies for a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome
question.explanation: Chaotic, multidirectional darting eye movements (opsoclonus) with myoclonus and ataxia make up the opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, which in a young child should prompt a search for a neuroblastoma. Calling it post-infectious ataxia ignores the defining eye sign. A lumbar puncture alone will not find the tumor. Normal reflexes argue against a Guillain-Barré variant, which does not cause opsoclonus.

sections.title: Telling central vertigo from peripheral
sections.content:
Vertigo is an illusion of movement, and the first localizing question is whether the illusion starts in the ear and its nerve or in the brainstem and cerebellum that read their signals. The time course, the eyes and the accompanying signs usually answer it.

**The time course**

An acute vestibular lesion begins abruptly and then fades as the brain compensates for the lost input (Pearl 2014, p. 119). Vestibular neuritis usually resolves over four to ten days (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Continuous dizziness that never fluctuates over long periods does not follow the vestibular pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 119).

**Nystagmus**

Of the nystagmus rules in [[m07-brainstem|Module 7]], two carry most of the weight here. Fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus but not central nystagmus, and pure vertical or pure torsional nystagmus is central (Brazis 2011, p. 265). In the most acute stage, fixation may fail to suppress even a peripheral nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 120), so look again later.

**The signs that come with it**

"Everything in neurology is based on the company you keep," and the rule applies with special force to central nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Hearing loss and tinnitus usually go with the ear (Pearl 2014, p. 119). Double vision, slurred speech, facial numbness and limb ataxia go with the brainstem and cerebellum. The figure above weighs the features the same way, and a single central feature overrules any number of peripheral ones.

:::deeper When the ear and the brainstem fail together
A stroke in the territory of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery breaks the hearing rule, because that artery supplies the inner ear as well as the brainstem. It can cause sudden one-sided deafness along with vertigo. In adults a bedside battery called HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus and a test of skew) is used to separate central from peripheral vertigo, though it has been studied far less in children.
:::

**Cerebellar infarct and tumor**

A cerebellar infarct can closely mimic acute labyrinthitis, with vertigo, nausea, vomiting and sometimes no limb ataxia. The usual clue is nystagmus that changes direction, found only if someone looks for it (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122). In children the central cause not to miss is a **posterior fossa tumor**, which is common in childhood (Pearl 2014, p. 63). Chiari and cerebellar malformations are the other common central causes of dizziness in children (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

**Recurrent spells in a child**

Brief, recurrent attacks have a different tempo and a different list of causes. Vestibular migraine is probably the commonest cause of recurrent vertigo in children (Brazis 2011, p. 354). Younger children may have **benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood**, probably a precursor of migraine. Its short spells, sometimes in clusters, leave the child frightened, pale and sweaty but fully aware (Brazis 2011, p. 355). An abnormal exam between spells calls for a search for a structural cause.
keyPoints: An acute vestibular lesion eases as the brain compensates, so unremitting dizziness that never fluctuates does not fit the vestibular pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 119).
Fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus but not central nystagmus, and pure vertical or torsional nystagmus is central (Brazis 2011, p. 265).
A cerebellar infarct can mimic labyrinthitis, and direction-changing nystagmus is the sign that gives it away (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122).
In children, a posterior fossa tumor is the central cause not to miss (Pearl 2014, p. 63; Brazis 2011, p. 355).
Brief recurrent spells with a normal exam in between suggest vestibular migraine or benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood (Brazis 2011, pp. 354-355).

question.question: A 7-year-old has had three days of vertigo and vomiting after a cold. Hearing is normal and finger-nose is accurate. Her nystagmus beats to the left on left gaze and to the right on right gaze. What should you do?
options: Diagnose vestibular neuritis and expect recovery within days
Perform a positional maneuver for benign positional vertigo
Reassure the family that this is benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood
Treat it as central and image the posterior fossa
question.explanation: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze is central (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122), and in a child the cause to exclude is a posterior fossa tumor (Pearl 2014, p. 63). Normal finger-nose does not reassure, because a cerebellar lesion can spare the limbs (Pearl 2014, p. 122). Neuritis nystagmus beats one way (Pearl 2014, p. 120), and childhood paroxysmal vertigo is brief (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

sections.title: The basal ganglia, from too little movement to too much
sections.content:
The cerebellum governs how accurately a movement is made. The basal ganglia govern how much movement occurs and which movement is chosen. Their disorders fall along a single axis, from **hypokinetic** disorders, with too little movement, to **hyperkinetic** disorders, with movements that should not be there (Pearl 2014, p. 116).

**Hypokinetic and hyperkinetic disorders**

- **Too little** movement shows as slowness, cogwheel rigidity, a tremor at rest, and a stooped, shuffling gait that cannot easily stop (Pearl 2014, p. 116). This is the adult Parkinson picture, and it is rare in childhood.
- **Too much** movement includes chorea (brief, random, flowing movements that dart from one body part to another), dystonia (sustained or repeated twisting postures, often provoked by a particular action), tics, myoclonus and athetosis. In children this end of the axis is far more common.

**Describing the movement**

There is no weakness to measure and often no change in the reflexes, so the movement itself has to show where the lesion is. Chorea, dystonia and a tremor at rest place the lesion in the subcortex and deep gray matter, the level the [[m03-first-fork|localizer]] assigns them to. Describe the movement precisely before you give it a name. Note what part moves, whether it is brief or sustained, random or patterned, at rest or on action, and whether it can be suppressed.

**Sydenham chorea**

The classic childhood example is Sydenham chorea, a post-streptococcal disorder that is a hallmark of acute rheumatic fever (Pearl 2014, p. 116). A school-aged child becomes fidgety and clumsy, drops things, cannot keep the tongue protruded and grips with a squeeze that waxes and wanes (the milkmaid grip), and behavior and mood often change too. The localization is the basal ganglia, and the diagnosis obliges you to look for the rest of rheumatic fever, including an echocardiogram, because carditis can be silent.

**Other childhood patterns**

Several other childhood patterns point to the same level but to very different mechanisms. They include dystonia that worsens through the day, as in dopa-responsive dystonia, dyskinetic cerebral palsy after injury to the deep gray matter around birth, and movement disorders that arrive with regression. They share a level, so the [[m11-where-to-what|tempo]] of the illness has to separate them.
keyPoints: Basal ganglia disorders sit on one axis, running from hypokinetic disorders with too little movement to hyperkinetic disorders with unwanted movement (Pearl 2014, p. 116).
In children the hyperkinetic end dominates, with chorea, dystonia, tics and myoclonus.
A movement should be described precisely, including which part moves, whether it is brief or sustained, random or patterned, and at rest or on action, before it is named.
Sydenham chorea is post-streptococcal and a hallmark of acute rheumatic fever, so the rest of the disease must be sought (Pearl 2014, p. 116).

question.question: A 9-year-old girl has three weeks of fidgety, irregular movements flitting between her hands, face and feet, a fluctuating hand grip, and new tearfulness. She had a sore throat six weeks ago. Strength and reflexes are normal. After placing the lesion in the basal ganglia, what is the most important next step?
options: Look for the other features of acute rheumatic fever, including the heart
Reassure the family that this is a tic disorder
question.explanation: Random, flowing movements that pass from one body part to another are chorea, and after a recent sore throat the leading cause is Sydenham chorea, a hallmark of acute rheumatic fever (Pearl 2014, p. 116). That diagnosis obliges a search for carditis. The spinal cord cannot generate chorea. Tics are patterned and briefly suppressible. Nerve conduction studies examine the motor unit, the wrong level here.

sections.title: Gait as the integrator
sections.content:
If you could watch a child do only one thing, choose walking. Gait is an excellent screen of the whole motor system (Pearl 2014, p. 114). Lesions at each level of the neuraxis impair it in a characteristic way, so a gait suggests both where the lesion is and what it probably is (DeMyer, p. 338). Working from muscle up to cortex (Pearl 2014, pp. 114-117) turns gait into a tour of the levels.

**Gait at each level**

- **Muscle** weakness gives a waddling, sway-backed gait from weak hip muscles, and the classic boy with Duchenne dystrophy has big calves, lordosis and a waddle (Pearl 2014, p. 115).
- **Junction** disease gives a gait that fatigues and recovers with rest.
- **Nerve** disease gives a steppage gait, with the knee lifted high to clear a dropped foot.
- **Root** disease gives an antalgic gait that avoids weight on a painful leg.
- **Cord** disease gives a stiff, scissoring gait from spasticity.
- **Basal ganglia** disease gives a dancing, choreic gait, or a shuffling one.
- **Cerebellar** disease gives a wide-based gait that cannot manage heel to toe.
- **Hemisphere** lesions give a circumducting gait, with the stiff leg swung outward.

Pick a gait in the figure above to see where it points.

**The developing gait**

The newborn steps reflexly when held upright, and this gives way to cruising along the furniture. Around the first birthday the toddler walks freely on a broad base, with short, jerky steps and frequent falls. The mature heel-toe stride with swinging arms comes later (DeMyer, p. 338). A broad-based, falling gait is normal at thirteen months and abnormal at five years.

**Toe walking**

Toe walking does not localize on its own. It can be the first sign of Duchenne dystrophy or of spastic diplegia, and it is seen in autism. In a child who runs, skips and hops normally, it may be an idiosyncratic, sometimes familial pattern with no disease at all (DeMyer, p. 338). The rest of the examination decides which of these it is.

**Examining gait**

Ask the child to walk, to run, to walk on the heels and on the toes, and to walk heel to toe. Heel and toe walking test the muscles of the sciatic territory as well as balance (DeMyer, p. 338). Young children cooperate better when the examination becomes a race or a game.
keyPoints: Gait screens the whole motor system, and its features suggest both the level and the cause of a lesion (DeMyer, p. 338; Pearl 2014, p. 114).

From the bottom up, the gaits are the waddle of muscle, the fatigable gait of the junction, the steppage of nerve, the antalgic gait of root, the scissoring of cord, the choreic gait of the basal ganglia, the wide-based gait of the cerebellum and the circumducting gait of the hemisphere.
A broad-based, falling toddler gait is normal around the first birthday (DeMyer, p. 338).
Toe walking does not localize on its own and may reflect Duchenne dystrophy, spastic diplegia, autism or an idiopathic familial pattern (DeMyer, p. 338).

question.question: A 4-year-old is referred for toe walking. He runs, skips, hops on either foot and can stand flat-footed. He rises from the floor without using his hands, his calves are normal in size, and reflexes and plantars are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Spastic diplegia from periventricular white-matter injury
An idiosyncratic or familial toe-walking pattern without neurological disease
question.explanation: A child who runs, skips and hops normally, rises without a Gowers maneuver and has normal tone and reflexes shows none of the serious causes, so this is idiosyncratic, sometimes familial toe walking (DeMyer, p. 338). Duchenne dystrophy would show proximal weakness and big calves. Spastic diplegia would bring stiff legs and brisk reflexes. A neuropathy causes foot drop, the opposite of toe walking.

quiz.question: A 12-year-old has a coarse tremor of the right hand that is absent at rest and grows larger as her finger approaches your finger. Which level does this tremor point to?
options: The right cerebellar hemisphere or its outflow
quiz.explanation: A tremor that appears on action and worsens near the target is an intention tremor, a cerebellar sign. Cerebellar signs lie on the same side as the lesion, so a right-hand tremor points to the right cerebellar hemisphere or its outflow. A basal ganglia tremor is present at rest, and a median nerve lesion causes weakness and numbness.

quiz.question: A 15-year-old started a new antiseizure medicine a week ago and is now unsteady, with slurred speech, nystagmus in every direction of gaze, and ataxia of all four limbs. Which reading fits best?
options: A pancerebellar syndrome from a drug effect
A lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
quiz.explanation: Symmetric cerebellar signs in all four limbs make a pancerebellar syndrome, which suggests a diffuse cause such as a drug (DeMyer, p. 339), and some antiseizure drugs also cause central-type nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121). A hemispheric tumor gives signs on its own side, and a midline lesion spares the limbs more. A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus cannot explain four-limb ataxia.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old stands steadily with her eyes open but sways and nearly falls when she closes them. Vibration and position sense are lost in the toes, and the ankle reflexes are absent. Finger-nose is accurate. What kind of ataxia is this?
options: Sensory ataxia from the large sensory nerves or dorsal columns
quiz.explanation: Steadiness with the eyes open that fails with them closed is a positive Romberg sign, because vision was compensating for lost position sense. With lost vibration and position sense and absent ankle reflexes, this is sensory ataxia from the large sensory nerves or dorsal columns. A child with cerebellar ataxia is unsteady with the eyes open too (DeMyer, p. 339).

quiz.question: A 10-year-old with high-arched feet lifts both knees high and slaps the feet down when walking. Ankle reflexes are absent and the calves are thin. Which level does the gait point to?
quiz.explanation: Lifting the knees high to clear dropped feet is a steppage gait, the gait of the peripheral nerve (Pearl 2014, p. 115). With high arches, thin calves and absent ankle reflexes it suggests a length-dependent, often inherited neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (DeMyer, p. 338). A cerebellar gait is wide-based, a cord gait stiff and scissoring, and a muscle gait a proximal waddle.

quiz.question: A 3-year-old has brief spells every few weeks: she suddenly looks frightened, clings to her mother, turns pale and sweaty, and cannot stand steadily, then is herself again within minutes. She stays responsive throughout. Her examination between spells is normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Focal seizures arising from the temporal lobe
quiz.explanation: Brief spells in which a young child looks frightened, pale and sweaty but stays aware, with a normal exam between them, match benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, probably a migraine precursor (Brazis 2011, p. 355). A posterior fossa tumor would leave signs between spells. Vestibular neuritis is a single episode lasting days (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Temporal lobe seizures would bring staring or automatisms.

opener.parable: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia don't move a limb by themselves. They shape movements that begin elsewhere and adjust their timing, force and smoothness. Damage to them can leave a child able to move but unable to move well.
opener.history: Gordon Holmes (1876–1965), whose scheme of examination underlies the one neurologists still use, described how a cerebellar patient breaks a movement into pieces, reaching the nose in two separate steps instead of one smooth curve.
